utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, good morning to you too and could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have the appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Carmela Javier, April Carter, and Barney Thomas for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning to all. Tina Drolec, Oonagh O'Connor, Boris Zorko, Chad Mair, Novak Lukic, Gregor Guy-Smith on behalf of Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And good morning to you, Mr. Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: My name is April Carter, and I'm here on behalf of the Prosecution and I have some questions to ask you about your testimony. The first topic I would like to discover is in relation to the special-purpose industry. I want to understand the organisations and the facilities involved. Let's take for example, Pretis. If Pretis were to want to establish a new line of materiels, what procedure would it go through in order to take it from the idea to the actual production?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly switch off unnecessary microphones. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First let's say that Pretis is a special-purpose industry in the Republika Srpska and it has nothing whatsoever to do with the special-purpose industry in the Republic of Yugoslavia, our procedure therefore do not apply to Pretis.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, what testing grounds were available in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia, there was a research and development institution with its own capacities and there were also three testing centres, the first one for land army, the second one for air force, and the navy testing centre for the navy.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you identify by name what those testing facilities were?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly switch off unnecessary microphones, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did tell you their names but they had their abbreviations as well. Would you be interested in those?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell me what Nikinci is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Madam Carter. I thought you were still dealing with the names of the companies.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, the witness asked you whether you want both the names and the abbreviations.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. I can certainly do it that way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, can you give us the names --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, just for a moment. With regard to Judge Moloto's focus, because of some of the distinctions that exist and some of the confusions that we've been having the past couple of days, are you taking the position that the testing centres and companies are the same? Because Judge Moloto's question was dealing with the names of companies and you indicated you were dealing with names of companies whereas previously you've been talking about names of testing facilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. I'm actually referring to the facilities themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good enough. Let's get the names.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me the the names of those facilities?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The land army had its testing facility and its name was abbreviated as TOC. The air force had its own testing facility in Batajnica. And when it comes to the navy, there was the navy testing facility. Those three were institutions that were dealing with the testing of equipment, both for domestically-produced equipment as well as for the equipment that came from imports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Kadijevic, what is the name of the navy testing facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The abbreviation was MOC, M-O-C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Now you've given us abbreviations. Give us the full names of all the facilities that you have given us acronyms of.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The full names for those three testing centre are as follows: The Technical Testing Centre of the Land Army, the Air Force Testing Centre, and the Navy Testing Centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, for purposes of the transcript and clarification, since he has just given us full names, I would suggest that we have initial caps, otherwise it doesn't look as if it's a name but rather a description of a place in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Stenographer, if you can take note of that. Thank you. Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know of a facility by the name of Nikinci, N-i-k-i-n-c-i?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with that facility. I was there a number of times. That's a technical testing facility for the testing of the land army equipment. It is some 80 kilometres away from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Who possesses this testing centre?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could not talk about the ownership of the facility but rather of the organisational structure of the entire army of Yugoslavia. That testing centre was part of the General Staff structure and it was affiliated with the assistant Chief of the General Staff for the land army. The assistant chief was its superior body.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated that this facility was used for testing of land army equipment. Was it used exclusively for the use of the testing of VJ land army equipment?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was also used for some equipment belonging to the air force that could not be tested elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Are you aware of it being used for the testing of any materiels coming from other special-purpose facilities such as Pretis?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, only because you have been previously discussing the former Yugoslavia, if we could have a time-frame within which this question is being asked, I think it would be of assistance to the witness and to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware between 1993 and 1995 the Nikinci Technical Testing Centre being used to test equipment -- or excuse me, test materiels from Pretis?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that centre was also used by Pretis. As well as all the entire special-purpose industry of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. In the production phase, the special-purpose industry tests its equipment internally at testing centres before it is delivered to the customer. If the result of the testing is positive, then the customer issues an order for the final testing of the equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I'd like to move on to another topic. You had testified yesterday -- or actually, on Monday, that the VJ and the General Staff had no competencies in relation to export of military equipment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, during 1993 to 1995 was it common for members of the MOD to meet with the leadership of special-purpose industries to explore their capabilities or capacities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: MOD of which country, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: During 1993 to 1995 was it common for members of the FRY MOD to meet with leadership of special-purpose industries to explore their capabilities or capacities?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Vague with regard to the issue of "common."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: During 1993 to 1995, did members of the FRY MOD meet with leadership of the special-purpose industries to explore their capabilities or capacities?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One of the principal tasks of the research and development administration is to ensure capacities for the production of materiel and equipment. It also invested funds for the adoption and development of new technologies, and that's why it had very close co-operation with all the companies and very frequent contacts with them. We had regular frequent meetings with all the state bodies, and when I say that, I mean other ministries as well as the managers of the special-purpose industries. At those meetings we analysed the situation, the contracts that were signed, and we also considered plans for the following year. That was a customary procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: How often would these meetings take place?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on the problem. There were directors with whom we would meet every fortnight. Whenever they had a problem, they wanted to consult with the Ministry of Defence. While I was chief of the research and development administration, I had to see them, I had to consider their proposals, and we had to discuss solutions. When we couldn't do that at my level, we went to the Ministry of Defence or to the ministry of the industry of either Serbia or Montenegro. So I would meet with the respective ministers or the ministers would come to our annual meetings in order to look at the possibilities of exercising all the necessary tasks to meet the needs of the state defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you were meeting with these directors, did you meet with the directors exclusively in Serbia and Montenegro, or did you meet with directors in the RS and the RSK as well?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have meetings with directors from RS and RSK as I did with the special-purpose production industries in Serbia. That was my duty, and I believe that I met with the director of Pretis on one or two occasions. His name was Milorad Motika, and I believe that we met at his request on a couple of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Would General Perisic have authority to explore special-purpose production capabilities and capacities with these directors?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Perisic did not have the staff structure within the General Staff that would be dealing either with the planning or research and development, therefore he did not need to meet up with the directors of special-purpose industries. And when we are talking about the meetings with directors, I hosted Mr. Perisic on two occasions when he toured some of the capacities. I was his escort. He wanted to look at the capabilities of those industries because the directors wanted us to sign contracts with them and the position of the government was that they were not capable of producing much; however, they showcased their products in their own facilities and that visit lasted about three hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicated that this occurred on two occasions. Can you tell us when those occasions were?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I have my usual problem with the years. I know that on the first occasion we went to Crvena Zastava and Kragujevac and the Krusevac base, Miloja Zakic, and the second time we went to the partisan factory in Uzice and the Cacak base Sloboda, and that could have been in 1997 or 1998 but I would sooner say that it was in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Would you have expected General Perisic to be involved in such matters in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Relevance as to Mr. Kadijevic's expectations.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has indicated that there was a clear bright line between the special-purpose factories falling under the MOD and the VJ's abilities within them, so what I'm trying to explore is what Mr. Perisic, during 1993 and 1995, had the capabilities for and the expectations of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand that last part of your answer, ma'am, whether Mr. Perisic during 1993 to 1995 had the capabilities for and the expectations of.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, indeed the witness has indicated that the -- that Mr. Perisic had no competencies whatsoever within the special-purpose industry, that barring the two times in which he served as host to Mr. Perisic in 1997 and 1998, that Mr. Perisic appears to have had no other contact. So I'm trying to explore that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, would you have had expectation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Go ahead, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In 1994 are you aware of Mr. Perisic touring any special-purpose facilities?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Given the structures that you've set out with relation to the special-purpose industries and the MOD as well as the VJ, would Mr. Perisic have had the competencies to go and tour and explore the special-purpose industry in 1994?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire General Staff including the Chief of the General Staff, Mr. Perisic, did not have any competencies with regard to the research, development, and production of military equipment. No competencies whatsoever. Those things are within the remit of the Ministry of Defence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Are you aware of General Mladic's competencies in relation to the special-purpose industries?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what special-purpose industries you mean. Are you referring to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or Republika Srpska? Where?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: We'll take those separately. Are you aware of General Mladic's competencies in relation to those special-purpose industries found in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that in Republika Srpska he had a certain degree of influence due to his authority. He did influence the special-purpose industry in Republika Srpska but in formal terms it [Realtime transcript read in error "he"] was the minister of defence that was in charge of the special-purpose in Republika Srpska just as its counter-part was in charge of the same type of industry in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And the second part of the question, are you aware of his competencies in relation to special-purpose industries found in the former Yugoslavia, the FRY?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic did not have absolutely any competencies with regard to the special-purpose industries in the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, on page 10, line 24, I believe there after the words "in formal terms" the word should be "it" and not "he" and I think we can probably agree upon that because it's recognised that General Mladic was not the minister of defence. I think that's probably just a transcription error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would agree with that. Madam Carter, I don't know what you think.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we would agree with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you. Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with Krusik in relation to the special-purpose industries?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me what it is?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a capacity or a holding company which consisted of several companies, and one of them, one of the most important one was the Krusik special-purpose industry. That company produced the programme of mortars and anti-tank guided missiles of the Maljutka type.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a gentleman by the name of Director Savic?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him when he was still director and later on when he was the assistant federal minister for the economy.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What was he director of?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a director of the entire Krusik company. And since the special-purpose industry was the most important part and the ownership of the rest of the companies when the transformation started, he was the number one man in that company, in Krusik.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicated he later became an assistant federal minister for the economy. Can you tell me which entity he was an assistant federal minister for?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The federal government appointed him assistant federal minister for the economy because he was an experienced businessman who had for a number of years led a very successful enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'll try to be more clear: Which country was he an assistant federal minister for?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could have been assistant federal minister only in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. There was no other federal state.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Where was Krusik located?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krusik is to the south-west of Belgrade, some 80 kilometres from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: As you are giving the directions in relation to Belgrade, can I assume that it's in the former -- excuse me, in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Serbia. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would seek leave to use a new document, XN422. This document is one of the extracts from the Mladic diaries. We have seen those extracts previously and Mr. Thomas and Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith spoke yesterday and there was an indication that there was an agreement, if the Court were to allow us to use such a document, that it would be tendered as an MFI document pending the decision of Your Honours in relation to the exhibits subject to the -- the motion for reconsideration of the Trial Chamber's order filed on 12 August 2010.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is in most of the terms correct, but there's only one issue which presents itself, which is if Ms. Carter could identify the purpose for which she seeks leave to use this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'd seek to use this document both for impeachment as well as for the truth of the contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think that there may need to be a bit of argument with regard to this. The argument will directly deal with some of the witness's testimony. It should be relatively brief, however, I don't think it would be appropriate for him necessarily to be in the room during the period of time that argument is being held, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could intervene at this moment. This, I thought, had been resolved. I think it can be resolved if I can have the opportunity to discuss this with my learned friends. I seek a brief adjournment for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would concur. Rather than there being anything where there's any confusion, I think that if we could have but a moment here, we may be able -- if Mr. Thomas warrants that he believes there can be resolution, I'm usually relatively confident that that is the case. We're hitting probably 85, 90 per cent. So if we could have a brief adjournment. I'm sure it wouldn't be any more than five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Court adjourned. We'll take a break and come back when the parties call us. --- Break taken at 9.34 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, I see you are on your feet, Mr. Guy-Smith is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I was just going to say I'd like to thank -- I think both parties would like to thank the Chamber for the opportunity to have had the discussion we've just had. Although it didn't clarify everything that we hoped to be able to clarify I think it clarified a sufficient amount that it leaves us in a position where we can have a crisp record on this issue because of the variety of legal matters that surround the whole question of what we generically call fresh evidence and its purpose. And I now will cede the microphone to Mr. Thomas, who is on his feet, or to Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would like to lay a full foundation for the request to use new evidence before the Chamber. The document that we are seeking to use is XN422, which is an extract of the Mladic diaries. As the Court is aware, we only received the Mladic diaries on 29 March of 2010.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter, may I interrupt you a little bit? Do we usually discuss them in open session?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Clarification has been made and, yes, we initially were using them in closed session or, excuse me, in private session; we are now able to speak about them in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is my understanding at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fine. I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As the Court is aware, we received these documents on 29 March of 2010. In relation to the extract that we are seeking to tender before the Court today, it was disclosed to the Defence on 5 May 2010 in B/C/S, and it was subsequently translated and disclosed on 11 May 2010 in English. As this document has been received by the Defence for over four months it was given in a language that both the defendant as well as many of the staff of the Defence team do understand on 5 May of 2010. We do believe that we have overcome any prejudice argument that the Defence may give. In relation to the document itself, we do believe that it is relevant, it goes directly to issues in relation to the special-purpose industry, it goes to the issues of Mr. Perisic's competencies in relation to that, as well as his contacts with that. So we would argue that it would be a relevant document to the Court's consideration, and because it is relevant we do believe it would in the interest of justice to be able to provide the Court with a full picture of the special-purpose industry, and so we would seek to use the new evidence here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And just to close up the circle, Madam Carter, you reiterate that you are -- the purpose for tendering it is both for impeachment and both for the truthfulness of the contents.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for your last question, Your Honour, with regard to the purpose for the tendering of this document, which Ms. Carter has indicated is both for impeachment and for the truthfulness of the contents. Obviously in discussions we've had previously with regard to the issue of fresh evidence, I think there's an appreciation and understanding that there are two distinct standards that exist, the standard for impeachment being a lower standard than the standard that one would apply and the Chamber would apply with regard to the Prosecution essentially re-opening their case through cross-examination. With regard to the issue of impeachment, I would suggest that Ms. Carter's position concerning impeachment is ill-advised. I take that position because of the testimony that was given at page 10, line 2, in which Ms. Carter asked the following question: "In 1994 are you aware of Mr. Perisic touring any special-purpose facilities?" The answer is: "I was not aware of that." If Mr. Kadijevic is now shown a document which establishes something different, that certainly wouldn't impeach him. It might give him information which he did not have before but it would not be impeachment. And I think it's important that we recognise that impeachment is not just putting up contradictory evidence but, rather, it's putting up evidence that in fact puts at issue the veracity of the assertion made by the witness. If the witness was not aware of the visit or Mr. Perisic's involvement, then it wouldn't be impeachment for that purpose. She has not indicated any other purpose of impeachment and in the failure to articulate specific grounds for impeachment, I would suggest, at least to the extent that I've taken the analysis thus far, that the application fails on those grounds by virtue of the fact it doesn't meet the definition. With regard to the second issue, which is being offered to prove the truth of the matter, of the contents, Ms. Carter has failed once again to meet the standard. The standard is one of exceptional circumstances. There's been no showing of exceptional circumstances with regard to the use of this document or this part of the Mladic diary at this time with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, is it not common knowledge between the parties and the Chamber that the Mladic diaries were obtained by both the Prosecution and the Defence after the close of the Prosecution case?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And was it not so that in fact there was an agreement to postpone the case for about a month, or even twice for that matter, to allow both parties to go through the Mladic documents to find out which of them either party might use?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is also an accurate statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. Now, if in those Mladic diaries the Prosecution finds documents that were not accessible to them during their case in chief, wouldn't they then be allowed to use them precisely for that reason? Doesn't that meet the standard?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, I do not believe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do not believe that if, as you've framed the question, Your Honour, that if in those Mladic diaries the Prosecution find documents that were not accessible to them during their case in chief, then they should be allowed to use them precisely for that reason because that doesn't deal with the ultimate issue which is the factual material that may exist within that document. And if that factual material exists in other places and if that factual material is material which is part and parcel of the Prosecution's case, then I don't believe that would necessarily meet the standards of exceptional circumstances. Just because something arrives which is new, does not in and of itself make it necessarily an exceptional circumstance for purposes of this particular analysis. For other analyses it may, but not for this particular analysis. We are talking about, thus far, special-purpose industry, that's something that we've been talking about for two years. We've been talking about testing facilities, that's something we've been talking about for two years. We're talking about Mladic, he is certainly somebody that we've been talking about for two years. We're dealing with issues concerning supply of materials; those are all matters that are -- have been an active, vibrant, and continued part of the Prosecution's case, and I don't think that just by asserting the conclusion one can find solace in the explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I follow your argument but let me say this to you: That indeed I agree with your assertions that all these topics have been spoken about for the last two years and the Prosecution has been seeking to prove these -- a certain position with respect to these topics for the last two years. This witness is testifying contrary to the position of the Prosecution. The Prosecution has used whatever other evidence they have had to state their position, and with respect to this witness, they seek to use this diary to endorse their position. So, one, it is not a new thing, these are not new topics to the Defence. These have been live issues between the parties for the last two years. And now the Prosecution is meeting this witness who is stating something contrary. And I take your point on the question of impeachment that the fact that he says he didn't know doesn't mean it didn't happen, therefore he could not be impeached by this document. But I think in that event it is properly within the competency of the Prosecution to say if you didn't know, sir, here is a document that says he did do so, if he did do so - I don't know what the document is going to say - and we can hear what he has got to say in response to that. To that extent therefore, the document does not introduce fresh evidence in fact because this has been a live issue for the last two years, as you've rightly said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand, I think, what your analysis is, I think I understand your analysis, and I think therein lies a particular problem. I'm going to walk away, just for a quick second, from the situation. If the issue in a case is whether or not the light was red or green, a witness gets up on the stand who was present at the location at the period of time when the issue comes up and is asked what question [sic] was the light and the witness says I believe the light was a green light. That's what I believe, that's what I was aware. Then there's information that is shown to the witness that the light was red. Now, that does not impeach that witness's -- that does not impeach that witness's belief, and since it does not impeach that witness's belief, the use of the evidence - which is the point - the use of the evidence to prove the truth of the matter asserted therein becomes the issue. When the propounding party says okay, here is a piece of evidence that the shows that the light was a colour other than which you believed it to be, that's the truth isn't it, the witness has no way of intelligently responding to it, the witness has no way of commenting on it outside of the confines of what their own knowledge is, and is being offered by the propounding party to prove something. Therein lies the rub. That's the problem. If the evidence is being offered for some other purpose other than to prove the truth of the matter asserted, then I would not be standing on my feet with regard to that issue. I think on the impeachment issue we are in agreement. With regard to the second issue, what is the value of this evidence? How do you value this evidence? Because ultimately what will occur is this: At the conclusion of the case the Prosecution will argue that this particular -- this particular document they seek to presently introduce, XN422, proves whatever they claim it proves. That evidence will be -- will have been given to you in the absence, in this situation, of testimony from somebody who was in a position because they are unaware of what is being discussed. That would be the vehicle that it comes to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure where you are going with your argument, Mr. Guy-Smith. I want to say to you, Madam Carter said she's tendering this document for two purposes; for purposes of impeachment and for purposes of the truthfulness of the content. You've put up your argument on impeachment, which I thought made sense and -- unless I hear the contrary from Madam Carter on that argument. And if she fails on that argument then it goes in for the truthfulness of it, but then from the point of view of the Prosecution, the Prosecution wants to put its position to this witness and assert its position. From the point of view of the truthfulness of the evidence, the Chamber will decide on it when it writes the judgement whether to believe the document or to believe the witness. That's where the perimeter ends. And in my view, I think the very fact of the circumstances under which this document was obtained, be it fresh evidence or not -- and I've indicated a little earlier that the topics that are being discussed here are not fresh evidence, they have been live issues between the parties for a long time, and you have said so yourself on the record -- it would qualify to go in even for the truthfulness of the content, whatever the Chamber will believe at the end. That's not the issue at this point. But having said that, Madam Carter, do you have anything to say on this point before we rule?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Briefly, Your Honour. If the world was as Mr. Guy-Smith has constructed and the only statement that was made by the witness in relation to the special-purpose industry was that he was unaware of this 1994 meeting, we would be in a much different position. However, at page 8, line 13, I specifically asked: "Would General Perisic have authority to explore special-purpose production capabilities and capacities with directors?" The witness responded: "General Perisic did not have the staff structure within the General Staff that would be dealing either with the planning or the research and development, therefore he did not need to meet up with the directors of special-purpose industries." Thus the witness has made a blanket statement that I seek to challenge. So I will argue that we are in a position in which he has set up a proposition that I seek to impeach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber rules that the objection -- I beg your pardon, where are we now? The document may be used even for the purpose of the truthfulness of the content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would now like to call up XN422. There are two B/C/S possibilities; we would seek to use the Latin transcript for the ease of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, it might be easier for Mr. Kadijevic to view it in hard copy. I have it in hard copy in both Latin and in Cyrillic. I'm happy to have this given to the usher so that Ms. Carter can take a look at them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no objection to their use.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, what you have before you is an extract from a diary of General Ratko Mladic. Before I ask you questions I just want to give you an opportunity to have a look over the document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Interpreters do not have copies of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I do have a single copy that I can provide for the interpreters and I'd also ask the Registrar if he could please scroll through the pages of the document for the ease of the Court as well. Your Honour, I do note the time. I'm not certain if Your Honours want to take the break at its normal time or continue to review the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, the Chamber does intend to take the break right now. We'll break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, in order to perhaps be able to speed things up, may I suggest that if the witness would like to have this particular document with him, he could review it over the break so he is in a position to take a look at it during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I have no objection to such a course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter. Well, thank you very much. I'm sure we'll be proficient in B/C/S by the end of the session. We don't have any English versions. We can look at it on the screen, Madam Carter, don't worry.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: General, I take it that you've had the opportunity to read through the document XN422 in its entirety; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, are you aware of the Ministry of Defence authorising General Perisic ever to meet with the Krusik RO?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two things there: First of all, the visit to Krusik and to a special-purpose industry facility is something that any minister can do without prior announcement, notice, or permission because these are not closed facilities, these are companies that exist within the economy of Serbia. And I highlighted yesterday that only some portions of those facilities produce for the Ministry of Defence and only those have a different regime. Sava Pustinja, assistant federal minister and chief of the military economic factory, informed me about this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: It indicates that both General Perisic as well as General Mladic, the two greatest generals, and their colleagues attended this meeting. If you are aware of the meeting, do you know who the delegation was?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was this meeting and I told you that my superior, Lieutenant-General Savo Pustinja, who was assistant minister of defence and chief of the military economic sector, attended this meeting and that after this meeting he briefly informed me about the content of the discussions they had at the meeting. As for this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Kadijevic, I'm sure you would like to go home as soon as possible, and for that reason, I would like us to -- I would like to ask you to please listen carefully to the question and answer succinctly to the question. The question was: Do you know who the delegation was? The correct answer should be yes, I know; no, I don't know. One of the two. Don't give a long story. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd asked you in the first session if you were aware of any meetings that General Perisic would have had with the special-purpose industry and you indicated at this time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am sorry, Madam Carter. You asked a question to which we really haven't had an answer. Do you know who the delegation was?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Outside of the minister that you've already named, are you aware of any of the additional delegates?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, because I never received any report.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you seem to know in great detail about this meeting as we sit here now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I object to the characterisation of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicate you now are aware of this meeting in 1994, however, when you spoke earlier, you indicated you were only aware of General Perisic attending the special-purpose industries in 1997 and 1998. What has jogged your memory to now recall 1994?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. Nothing jogged my memory. I told you that in 1997 he went in my organisation. I organised such a meeting for Mr. Perisic. I was the organiser and I met him at the factory. As for this meeting, I didn't take part in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: As it's now evident that you are aware of this 1994 meeting, are you aware of any other meetings that General Perisic attended at the special-purpose industry, whether you were his host or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember but I remember that I accompanied General Pustinja when, together with General Mladic, we visited Crvena Zastava plant.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicated that you attending Crvena Zastava plant with General Mladic. Was that one of the 1997 or 1998 meetings?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So beyond the -- so now we have two meetings in 1994, a meeting in 1997, and a meeting in 1998. Are there any others that you recall?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I am sorry. Because of the nature of what we are discussing if we could have a more particular question. So we now have two meetings in 1994. We are putting a bunch of meetings together. Are these meetings that he is aware of, meetings that he was informed of, meetings he was involved in? Because they all are different and require potentially different analysis and different questions that could come on redirect, and rather than bunching everything together --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I don't understand what you are saying. What has been bunched together? The Prosecution has just mentioned the number of meetings, not sort of saying they are all similar. I don't know what your objection is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The problem is, because as a reader, if I start at line 21 I have the witness attending a meeting in 1994. If I'm the reader and I continue with line 24, I now have him involved in four meetings, which is not the state of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, this witness has told us that he hosted Mr. Perisic on a meeting that he organised to this company sometime in whatever the year was. He has also told us that Mr. Mladic went there sometime in 1994. He has told us of a meeting in 1997, I don't know remember what in 1998. I think I will overrule you. If you have any clarifications you want to make on these meetings you can do so on re-examination. This is no point of objection. Continue Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, during your proofing session, were you shown this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the document, beginning on page 1 we have General Perisic speaking where he says that: "We have come to see what we can do to help the Republika Srpska army and how."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do apologise, what we have on page 1 are notations from a third party as to what the third party claims General Perisic says as opposed to what we have General Perisic saying. And I take exception with the idea that now the document becomes self-authenticating with regard to what my client says, because it is not. These are notes from a third party. And if they were characterised in that fashion, I have no objection. But to take the position this is what he says is grossly inaccurate and there's no way to test it unless the Prosecution is intending on bringing General Mladic to these proceedings for purposes of testifying against Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'm happy to rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: General, at page 1 a statement is attributed to General Perisic in which he is to have said: "We have come to see what we can do to help the Republika Srpska army and how." What authority did General Perisic have in order to help the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Once again, I have a problem here. The problem is with regard to what is attributed here. First of all, I think it's important for us to have an understanding of whether or not the witness knows whether or not General Perisic said this or didn't say this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Overruled.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir. I'll repeat my question. Under what authority did General Perisic have to help the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'll interpose one final objection with regard to this line of questioning because I think we are going to have the same problem, which is that if it assumes facts not in evidence, the facts not in evidence being that he did in fact make this statement, so in the absence of having some understanding as to whether or not the information contained in the diary as it is constituted is accurate, assumptions that are being made, whether you are talking about factual or legal conclusions to be drawn, are not only confusing, they are misleading and they do not establish in any way the kind of record that allows for the Defence to counter such evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can deal with that in re-examination. Madam Carter, continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's my problem, Your Honour, unfortunately I can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've ruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- because I don't have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have ruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate, and I have a record to make. I have a record to make now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you have problems with my ruling, go and appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I can't deal with it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the recourse.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand but I can't deal with it on re-examination. If I could deal with it on re-examination, I would. Otherwise, I wouldn't be protesting as vigorously as I am right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, please take your seat. Please take your seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I trust you understand that there's a problem we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please take your seat, sir. If you have a problem, you resolve the problem. If you have an objection, you raise an objection. The Chamber doesn't rule on your problems. Please take your seat. I have ruled. The Chamber has ruled, Mr. Guy-Smith, please take your seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I will, and I did raise an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, please take your seat. Thank you. Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, under what authority did General Perisic have to help the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already stated when it comes to the production of armament and military equipment and procurement from those companies, General Perisic didn't have absolutely --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... answer the question specifically was under what authority, and since the witness is not answering the question, that being the question of authority, I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, this is your witness and he answers the way he answers. You can't object to the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We've been through this before, as a matter of fact, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We have been through this before indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And previously, as a matter of fact, on a number of occasions when Mr. Harmon took exception to a witness's answer, you upheld his objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter, will you proceed, please. Mr. Kadijevic, you were in the process of answering. Can you please answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If you can continue your answer. Under whose authority would General Perisic have to help the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Perisic worked based on the authorities that he had as a Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia and the competencies and tasks given to him by the Supreme Defence Council. I was not in a position to know what instructions had the Supreme Defence Council given to the Chief of Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. In the ministry where I worked, I was not privy to that kind of information.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, are you indicating that the Supreme Defence Council could have authorised General Perisic to take on such matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: False speculation on his part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not what is he indicating, Madam Carter. He is just telling you the authorities that Mr. Perisic had so far as he knows.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of under what authority General Perisic might have been able to make a statement in relation to what can be delivered with and without payment? Under whose authority would he be able to do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think this question has been asked and answered, Madam Carter. That is the authority under which he acted would be the authority under which he would ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'll move to page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, on page 4 it indicates that in this meeting they "resolved the matter for fuses for aerial bombs." Are you aware -- after the discussions with your minister after this meeting, are you aware of any authority that General Perisic would have been given in order to engage in these kinds of resolutions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter, I think the question of authority has been exhausted.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'll move to the final page of the document. Excuse me, it must be the preceding page. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, some final comments are being attributed to General Perisic. One of them is that: "We will see how much we can set aside for you from our reserves." Do you know what the term "reserves" means in this context?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You say the preceding page. Is that page 3?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it's the page that's on the screen, page 7.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it says "reserves," I believe that these are war reserves at the disposal of the Army of Yugoslavia in its depots, the reserves of materiel in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In relation to the war reserves held by the VJ army -- excuse me, VJ, was it within General Perisic's competence to be able to set aside from his own reserves?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The federal government was the owner of those reserves. Those reserves were property of the Republic of Yugoslavia. Those materiels and equipment were given to the Army of Yugoslavia for its use.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of a decision that was taken in 1994 by the Supreme Defence Council where General Perisic was authorised to supply the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres with materiel?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see a document of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Do you know what the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres are?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 30th and the 40th Personnel Centres were established with a view to maintain the list of those officers of the Army of Yugoslavia who were referred or assigned to serve in the RS and VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In the RS and VRS. I am not sure whether you have been correctly interpreted. The interpretation says these officers were assigned to serve in the RS and VRS. We understand RS to stand for Republika Srpska, VRS to stand for the Army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said the Army of Republika Srpska and the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicated that you saw a document to that effect. Sir, are you indicating that you are aware that General Perisic had the authority given to him by the SDC to supply the 30th and 40th Personnel Centre members who were serving in the RS and the RSK; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the document was issued, I didn't see it. I was not aware of its contents. I didn't know it existed. The Defence counsel told me about that session of the Supreme Defence Council and showed me this particular document for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And speaking of seeing documents for the first time, can you tell me, when is the first time that you saw the extract from the Mladic diaries?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which extract, this one on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, no, the previous -- yes, Your Honour, the one on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you tell me the first time that you saw that document?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've not seen it before today.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If I can have one moment to consult with co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you discussed yesterday and the day before the VTI, the Military Technical Institute; is that the right acronym?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Who is the employer of personnel serving in the VTI?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The VTI employed people pursuant to the openings to which people applied. People who applied were citizens of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and if they met the criteria with regard to their previous experience with research and development, they were selected. Their applications were approved and their employment was approved by the Ministry of Defence. The Ministry of Defence wanted to curb, to limit the number of the VTI employees.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Apologies, Your Honour, before I had moved on to this new topic, I intended to tender Exhibit XN422 into evidence as an MFI'd document -- not as MFI, Your Honour, simply as an admitted document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as I think the Chamber is clear, we object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P2928. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, moving back to the topic we just began, you are indicating that the employer of the personnel serving in the VTI would be the Ministry of Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Do you know of a workshop given the monicker VTI013?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the question again?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would like to know if he is aware of a workshop with the name VTI013.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that the VTI had a workshop where they crafted models and prototypes of simpler pieces of equipment. I'm not familiar with its number because each part of the institute had a coded number which consisted of some letters and some figures, so I wouldn't be able to confirm that the number that you just -- or the name you just mentioned was the name or the designation of that particular workshop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I ask you again, Mr. Kadijevic; the answer would have been, "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Is it fair to assess that if a facility has VTI in its title, however, it is still an MOD facility?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Could General Perisic exercise any power over personnel serving there?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Perisic could not exercise power over any of the facilities of the VTI or the whole VTI as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'm actually referring to the personnel that are serving there. Would General Perisic be able to exercise any power over the personnel serving in the VTI?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Would he have the authority to deploy personnel serving there?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not have that authority. Only for the director of the institute. The director had to be a general. At the Supreme Defence Council meeting he could exert his influence in order to either have that person approved by a decree or disapproved for the particular position.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'd like to bring up P2721 on to the screen. Your Honour, it's evident that this first page is going to be extremely hard for the witness to read on the screen. I do have hard copies of the document. I would indicate that on the final page -- on the final page that I have copied, I have made a single highlighting. Unfortunately, I don't have a secondary copy. I'm happy to provide this to the witness at the discretion of the Defence, or if they have a clean copy, I'm happy to provide that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Show the Defence the document, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If I can ask the court personnel to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Court Usher, will you please wait for the document so that you can take it away.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't have on the record there is reaction of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I nodded my agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We would like to have it --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Sorry, Madam Interpreter, you were saying something? We spoke simultaneously and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge. Interpreter's note: Interpreters do not have copies of the document that is being used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We understand that. Can the interpreters please be provided with a copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm asking the assistance of Ms. Javier to get copies as soon as possible for the interpreters' booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, the document that you have before you indicates that it's from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, it's delivered to the Chief of General Staff of the Yugoslav Army, that would be General Perisic -- no, excuse me, that would be the chief that was Mr. Perisic's predecessor; is that correct? Actually, sir, could you do me a favour? The third line of the document gives a date. Can you please tell me, in the original, what is the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 16 May 1995. That's the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And on May 16th of 1995, who was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's okay. Thank you, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the court staff, yes, I am seeking the translation to 0647-6755, the first translation available in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, on 16 May 1995, who was the Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say 1995, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not 1993? The date of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there appears to be a typo in the document. The original indicates 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We can't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I can't read it either, and I would appreciate it if Ms. Carter wouldn't testify.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: With all due respect to Mr. Guy-Smith, I had the witness confirm and read the date and I'm using the testimony of the witness himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The reason I said what I said is because as I'm looking at the document in English, it says at the very beginning of the document, it says 16/5/1993 and then at a later point in time it has the date of 1995. So there are both dates contained in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam -- we are looking at this date at its largest. It's zoomed to a very huge figure. It could be either.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, the witness actually has a copy that has been copied where you can actually see the document much better. I'm happy to ask, if the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can confirm with the witness. Just ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We've now enlarged the document as much as we can in the original and it looks like a 3. It looks like the date is 16.5.1993. And obviously Ms. Carter appreciates the importance of this because if this is a document in 1993 in the month of May, then this is a document that concerns a matter which would not have been within Mr. Perisic's purview because he was not the Chief of the General Staff at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, the Chamber has just indicated that it has also looked at it and that this number could be either a 5 or a 3. It's indeterminable from looking at it and anybody can come and look at it here or we can look at it elsewhere. This Chamber is not able to determine, but if this witness is able to tell us, Madam Carter can ask the question and it's up to the witness to tell us if he can see anything, and if he can't, he can't. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate that. But I don't think that this is a situation in which necessarily having the witness make a determination of the date is appropriate. If he has no familiarity -- as of yet we have not established that he has any familiarity with the document, that he was the author of the document, that he has ever seen the document before, that he has had any contact at all with this document. So for at this point in time for him to do the same thing that we are doing, I think would be inappropriate with regard to the date itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: General, can you please again read the third line of the document that you have in your hand in regards to the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can the document that the witness is reading be provided for the review of the Chamber and then brought back to the witness. Actually, for transparency, if it can again be shown to Mr. Guy-Smith before the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. My eyes fail me. I'm still not in a position to tell what the number is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's appreciated, Mr. Guy-Smith. Join the club.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, this document indicates that the VRS is seeking authority -- specifically, General Mladic is seeking authority from the Chief of General Staff to engage Zoran Stojkovic from the VTI. Can you tell me, are you aware of any circumstances where the VRS would make specific request to the Chief of General Staff for VTI personnel beyond the one that we are looking before us?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had similar cases. There were requests to engage VTI experts, if that's what was needed by the VRS army. After this request that was received by the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, there would be a letter to the Ministry of Defence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as the superior body to the VTI.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, just below to the bottom right of the seal found on top of this document, there's some handwriting. Can you tell me what that handwriting says?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "To be approved," and I believe that I can see the initials of General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Move to the second page of the document. And I would seek translation 0647-6756.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, the second document is an approval by the General Staff in relation to the engagement of Zoran Stojkovic. Is this approval consistent with the note that you read on the first page approving this deployment?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the response that we saw on page 1, and this was written by the office of the Chief of the General Staff to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If we can now move to the third page. And English translation -- pardon. Hold one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Prior to moving on to the next document, sir, can you please tell us, within the first line there's an indication that this document is referring to a preceding document. Can you tell us the date of that preceding document?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the heading or the first sentence in the second document?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In the second document, the paragraph begins, "In regards to your request ..." and gives a telegram confidential number. Can you tell me --

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 16 May 1995 is the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And can you tell me, does the confidential number given, 10/33-1-121, also correspond with the first page?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If we can now move to the third page, and translation 0647-6757.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, this indicates that Zoran Stojkovic, who was on duty at Military Technical Institute, would be temporarily sent to the 30th Personnel Centre. If you are aware, can you tell me where this person was being sent?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order for this task to be carried out, Stojkovic was first being sent to the 30th Personnel Centre, which is where officers were sent within the Army of Yugoslavia in order to send them to the VRS to serve there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If we can now move to the fourth page, doc ID 0647-6758.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell me what Zoran Stojkovic was being sent to the VRS to do?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was temporarily engaged on training snipers in the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And if we can move to the following page, doc ID 0647-6759.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, is the document before you a report from Zoran Stojkovic on his time in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a report signed by him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The VJ engaged this gentleman to carry out the psychological -- excuse me, sent him to the VRS in which he carried out psychological preparation of these snipers, didn't he? Line 5.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: He also trained them, and it "... proved to be more efficient in the combat operations which resulted in the high combat morale, less expenditure of ammunition, and a large number of hit soldiers on the enemy side." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And moreover him just being a sniper trainer, he was also going to train the instructors of other sniper trainers, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And this was all being done in the VRS in the summer of 1995, was it not?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If we can move to the following page. That would be English translation 0647-6760.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, when these individuals were serving in the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres they were VJ officers still, weren't they, or VJ employees, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would object to plurality here since we are looking at a particular document and we are dealing with a particular individual. If she is referring to the individual that we've been speaking about, Stojkovic, I don't have any objection to the question as propounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I intended to go broad than particular but I'm happy to stick with the specific Mr. Stojkovic for this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, when Mr. Stojkovic served in the Army of the Republika Srpska, at that time he was still a VJ employee, was he not?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked in the Military Technical Institute where he had a permanent status. He was sent to the 30th Personnel Centre, which was basically subordinated to the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, on a temporary basis. He was temporarily sent there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, are you indicating that this gentleman was temporarily in the chain of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, temporarily.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You mentioned earlier that this was not a singular instance. How often did General Perisic engage members of the VTI to serve in the VJ or the personnel centres?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't claim with certainty how many, but I know that I solved problems together with the director of the Military Technical Institute when a request would be sent from the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska to the Ministry of Defence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. We would not send them to the 30th Personnel Centre on those occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked how often General Perisic sought VTI members for temporary deployment in the VJ. Can you tell me how often that occurred?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you that. This example here is a surprise to me too. I was not aware of these cases. And you can see based on the correspondence that these documents did not go via the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other cases where deployment -- temporary deployment in the VJ took place where the documents didn't circulate through the MOD?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware because in principle we would use the experts from the Military Technical Institute outside of that institution only on -- in exceptional cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of any other instance beyond this gentleman where a VTI member was temporarily deployed to the VJ?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Isn't that badgering the witness? He has just answered the question, Madam Carter. Are you aware of any other cases where temporary deployment in the VJ took place where the documents didn't circulate through the MOD, isn't that the same question?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm trying to remove the MOD circumvention. I'm just asking generally. We still haven't gotten an answer to that question, the general question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Are you aware of other instances where VTI members were deployed temporarily into the VJ?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We haven't had a translation of the answer, Interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just repeat your answer, please, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said clearly that I'm not aware of other cases where members of the Military Technical Institute were sent to the 30th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not what you said. You said "ne." What you said was "ne." That's what was not translated. That's fine. Carry on, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You separated out the 30th Personnel Centre. Can you tell me, are you aware of any other deployments to the VJ as a whole?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC [Resumed]
